title: Private Caregiver March
subject: Constitutional Law
stem: Mary is the director of a private association of home-health nurses that holds an annual public march under a chosen theme honoring bedside caregivers. The association obtains a city parade permit and selects its signs, speakers, and order of marchers. The city orders the association to include a private group carrying a banner stating that home-health care exploits families and should end, even though Mary says the banner would change the association's message.
call: What is the association's best First Amendment argument?

choices.A: The association loses unless it proves that the criticizing banner is obscene.
choices.B: Forced inclusion may violate the organizer's right not to alter its expressive message.
choices.C: A public march is never expressive because it includes walking.
choices.D: The city may compel inclusion because the route uses public streets.

rightExplanation: A private parade or march can be expressive even though it uses streets and ordinary movement. When the organizer selects a theme and controls the message, the government generally may not force the organizer to include a private speaker whose message would alter the organizer's own expression. The association's best argument is compelled speech: the city order would require it to carry a message it does not choose to convey.

wrongExplanations.A: Obscenity is a separate category of unprotected speech. The association's claim does not depend on proving that the opposing banner is obscene.
wrongExplanations.C: A march can convey a message through its theme, signs, speakers, and selection of participants. Physical movement does not defeat expressive character.
wrongExplanations.D: Public-street use gives the city authority to regulate logistics, but it does not eliminate a private organizer's editorial discretion over its own expressive event.
